parsed_answer.content:
When architecting modern enterprise systems in the Java ecosystem, developers frequently encounter Spring Boot and Spring Cloud, two pillars of the broader Spring ecosystem that serve entirely distinct architectural tiers. Spring Boot is an opinionated convention-over-configuration framework designed to streamline the bootstrap, packaging, and execution of standalone, production-grade Spring applications. It eliminates the boilerplate of XML configurations, manual dependency management, and embedded server setup by auto-configuring beans based on classpath inspection and providing out-of-the-box starters.

Spring Cloud, on the other hand, is an orchestration and governance layer built on top of Spring Boot. While Spring Boot makes it trivial to build a single microservice, Spring Cloud solves the complex distributed systems problems that arise when you have dozens or hundreds of those microservices communicating across a network. It provides unified abstractions and tooling for service discovery, dynamic configuration management, circuit breaking, smart routing, and distributed tracing. Therefore, Spring Boot is the foundational runtime vehicle, whereas Spring Cloud is the distributed systems toolkit engineered to run multiple such vehicles cohesively.

items: Spring Boot leverages the Spring Framework's ConditionEvaluator to dynamically parse @ConditionalOnClass and @ConditionalOnMissingBean annotations, spinning up embedded Tomcat, Jetty, or Undertow servers only when relevant web dependencies are present.

Spring Cloud operates via SpringFactoriesLoader mechanisms to load context initializers, enabling property source bootstraps from remote repositories like a Spring Cloud Config Server before the main application context even refreshes.

Spring Cloud Netflix and OpenFeign abstract low-level HTTP client mechanics, using dynamic interface proxies to inject ribbon-based load balancing and declarative REST client execution directly into the Spring Boot bean container.

parsed_answer.content: A classic production anti-pattern is mismanaging the Spring Cloud version train relative to the underlying Spring Boot version. Spring Cloud releases are tied to specific Spring Boot releases via BOMs (Bill of Materials). Upgrading Spring Boot in a microservice without checking the corresponding Spring Cloud release train compatibility will instantly break context initialization due to mismatched auto-configuration SPI entries and deprecated property bindings.

title: What is the difference between Spring Cloud and Spring Boot?
